summary: Luke tells Theophilus why he wrote: he has carefully traced the eyewitness accounts of Jesus so that Theophilus may be certain of what he was taught.
key_insight: Luke opens his Gospel with a method, not a miracle: eyewitnesses, careful research and an orderly account. In Greek his long opening sentence ends on the word “certainty.” He wants faith in Jesus to stand on what really happened.
story: Many had already taken in hand to set in order a narrative of “those things which have been fulfilled among us.” They wrote down what had been handed on by men who “from the beginning were eyewitnesses and ministers of the word.”
Luke decided to write as well. He had followed the whole story closely from the very first, and he set out to write “an orderly account” for a man he addressed as “most excellent Theophilus.”
His purpose was plain: “that you may know the certainty of those things in which you were instructed.”

scene.label: A historian’s opening
scene.text: Greek historians and medical writers of Luke’s day often began with a formal preface about earlier works, sources and purpose. Luke’s four verses are one long, polished sentence in Greek. From verse 5 his style changes and begins to sound like the Old Testament, as the story moves to a priest in Jerusalem.

scene.label: “Most excellent”
scene.text: The same title is given to the Roman governor Felix in a letter Luke records (Acts 23:26). Theophilus was probably a man of some rank, and he had already been taught about Jesus. Luke addresses him again at the start of Acts (Acts 1:1).

scene.label: The earlier accounts
scene.text: Luke does not name the “many” who wrote before him. Most scholars think Mark’s Gospel was one of them, since much of Mark’s material appears in Luke. Luke does not criticize these writers; he adds his own careful account.

scene.label: Who Luke was
scene.text: Paul calls him “the beloved physician” (Colossians 4:14). Luke was not an eyewitness of Jesus, but he traveled with Paul, and in Acts he writes “we” for those journeys. He went with Paul to Jerusalem (Acts 21:17) and sailed with him from Caesarea two years later (Acts 24:27; 27:1). Those years in Judea may well be when he talked with eyewitnesses.

witnesses.luke: Only Luke opens with a word about his own method. The other Gospels plunge straight into their story; Luke first tells Theophilus how and why he wrote. The preface may well introduce both his Gospel and Acts, and it explains the care he takes to name rulers, places and dates (Luke 2:1–2; 3:1–2).

seeing.reveals: Jesus is not an idea or a legend. Luke presents Him as a real person in real places, whose life fulfilled what God had promised, seen by people who walked with Him and then served His word.
seeing.living: Luke wrote for a man who had already been taught and needed certainty. If you believe but sometimes wonder whether it is all true, Luke invites you to read the record and weigh the witnesses. Faith in Jesus does not ask you to stop thinking.
seeing.ponder: What would change in the way you pray and speak about Jesus if you were certain, not merely hopeful, that these things happened?

preaching.big_idea: Faith in Jesus rests on real events, faithfully witnessed and carefully written down.
preaching.watch_for: Notice the words that build Luke’s case: “fulfilled,” “eyewitnesses,” “orderly,” “certainty.” His Gospel ends with Jesus telling His followers, “you are witnesses of these things” (Luke 24:48).
